directions: Set rhizome divisions shallowly in fall, just as autumn rains resume, into humus-rich but fast-draining soil beneath open oak or conifer canopy. Yellowleaf iris comes from the mixed woodlands of southwestern Oregon and the northern California coast ranges, where it survives bone-dry summers under a thin duff layer, so avoid any supplemental irrigation once the plant is dormant in summer. Flowers are pale cream to lavender with fine purple veining and appear on short stems in mid-spring, best appreciated at close range along a shaded path edge. Leave clumps undisturbed for several years, as this species resents frequent transplanting and flowers more freely once well established.

Plant rhizome fans shallowly in fall into lean, sharply drained soil, ideally on a gentle slope that sheds winter moisture; Siskiyou iris is endemic to the serpentine-influenced soils and open woodlands of the Klamath-Siskiyou region straddling the Oregon-California border, and it demands a completely dry summer dormancy to thrive. Its deep golden-yellow flowers, heavily netted with maroon-brown veining, rise above unusually broad, leathery, evergreen leaves that distinguish it from most other Pacific Coast iris species. Give it full sun to light open shade and resist the urge to water or fertilize once bloom finishes in late spring, since summer moisture promotes rot in this drought-adapted species.

Divide and reset rhizomes shallowly in fall beneath the dappled canopy of mixed evergreen or closed-cone pine forest, mimicking the shaded North Coast Range and Klamath habitats where Purdy's iris naturally grows. Its ivory to pale cream flowers are dramatically veined and dashed with maroon-purple, held just above tufted evergreen foliage in mid to late spring, and show best where a bit of dappled light filters through overhead branches. This species is one of the more shade-tolerant Pacific Coast irises, but like its relatives it must dry out completely through summer, so plant it away from irrigated lawns or beds and let natural rainfall carry it once established. Avoid heavy mulch or soil amendments that hold moisture against the rhizomes.

Set divisions shallowly in fall into fast-draining soil under open oak woodland or grassy slopes, the classic habitat of this low, ground-hugging iris found from the Coast Ranges south of Mendocino down into the Sierra Nevada foothills. Flower color is famously variable across its range, spanning cream, yellow, lavender, and blue-violet, all carried on very short stems atop an unusually long floral tube, the source of its common name bowltube iris. Because the flowers sit nearly at ground level, site it where it can be viewed up close, such as a border edge or a naturalized slope, and give it a hot, dry summer rest with no irrigation once the foliage begins to fade. It tolerates heavier clay better than some Pacific Coast iris relatives provided drainage improves markedly by early summer.

Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in the light shade of pine or oak duff, echoing the lower montane forests of the Sierra Nevada foothills where this species is native. Sierra iris tolerates a bit more winter cold and occasional light snow cover compared with its lowland coastal relatives, but it demands the same absolutely dry summer dormancy once its pale yellow to cream flowers finish blooming in late spring. Grow it on a slope or raised bed where winter rain drains away quickly, and resist watering through summer even during hot, dry spells, since the rhizomes rot readily in damp soil during dormancy. It combines well with other dry-shade Sierra foothill natives such as manzanita and ceanothus.

Set rhizome fans shallowly in fall into humus-rich, fast-draining soil beneath oak or bay woodland canopy, matching the shaded Coast Range habitat of this iris found from Napa County south through the Santa Cruz Mountains. Its pale creamy-yellow flowers, only faintly veined, are more subtly marked than many Pacific Coast iris relatives and appear in mid-spring above evergreen, grass-like foliage. Fernald's iris tolerates more shade than most of its relatives and appreciates a leaf-litter mulch that mimics the forest floor, but it still requires a completely dry summer rest with no irrigation once flowering ends. Leave established clumps undisturbed, dividing only when flowering noticeably declines.

Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in fall in well-drained soil near a partly shaded slope or streambank setting, reflecting the foothill canyon habitat of the Kaweah and Tule River drainages of Tulare and Kern counties where this rare iris is endemic. Munz's iris is prized as the bluest of all the Pacific Coast irises, producing striking lavender-blue to true blue-violet flowers on taller stems than most relatives in mid-spring. Because wild populations grow along seasonal streamcourses, it tolerates slightly more moisture in winter and early spring than other Pacific Coast species, but it still must dry out substantially through summer to avoid rhizome rot. Give it excellent drainage, some afternoon shade in hot inland gardens, and protect it from prolonged freezes, since its native range rarely sees hard winter cold.

Set rhizome divisions shallowly in fall into lean, sharply drained soil beneath open oak or pine woodland, the typical setting for this iris across the inner north Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills of California. Long-tubed iris is closely related to bowltube iris and shares its narrow, grass-like evergreen leaves, but bears especially slender flower segments and an exceptionally long floral tube behind pale cream to soft yellow blooms in spring. Give it full sun to light open shade and a bone-dry summer dormancy with no supplemental water, since it comes from sites that receive essentially no rain from May through October. It is best used in a naturalized dry meadow or rock garden planting alongside other summer-dormant California natives rather than in a regularly irrigated bed.
